title: The Buccaneers may have found their offensive identity against Dallas
description: Tampa Bay rushed for 241 yards against Dallas, giving rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels the support he needed to secure his first NFL victory.
fullText:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers spent the first four weeks of the 2026 NFL season searching for an offense they could rely on. Thursday night's 24-16 victory over the Dallas Cowboys may have provided the clearest picture yet of what that offense should look like, especially with undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels under center.

Tampa Bay finished with a season-high 241 rushing yards, averaging 6.2 yards per carry, and totaled 419 yards of total offense. It was a significant change for a team that had struggled to sustain drives and finish games during its 0-4 start. Rather than asking Daniels to carry the offense through the air, the Buccaneers established their running game and used it to create opportunities throughout the night.

Bucky Irving was the driving force behind that success, rushing for a career-high 165 yards and a touchdown on 21 carries. His 72-yard run to open the second half immediately put Dallas on its heels, setting up Emeka Egbuka's 14-yard rushing touchdown on the following play. Irving also caught a five-yard touchdown pass in the second quarter, finishing with 175 yards from scrimmage and two scores.

The performance wasn't simply the result of one explosive run. Tampa Bay repeatedly turned to Irving and its rushing attack to keep the offense moving, including a critical 23-yard carry late in the fourth quarter that helped the Buccaneers run out the clock. Irving's production gave Tampa Bay a reliable option when it needed yards, something that had been missing during the team's losing streak.

Daniels benefited from that balance, completing 19 of 25 passes for 189 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. His 110.2 passer rating represented a considerable improvement over his two-interception debut against Green Bay. He also connected with Tez Johnson on a 64-yard completion in the third quarter, helping set up Irving's one-yard touchdown run that extended Tampa Bay's lead to 21-10.

Perhaps the most encouraging sequence came much earlier. After Dallas scored on its opening possession, Daniels responded by leading a 15-play, 73-yard touchdown drive that consumed 10 minutes and 58 seconds. The rookie completed all eight of his passes during the possession, which ended with Irving's touchdown reception. According to Scott Smith of Buccaneers.com, it was the second-longest scoring drive in franchise history.

That possession demonstrated something Tampa Bay had struggled to accomplish through four games: controlling the pace without relying on a single explosive play. The Buccaneers kept their defense on the sideline, converted key downs, and answered an early Dallas touchdown without letting the game get away from them.

The performance also raises an important question for offensive coordinator Zac Robinson. Tampa Bay has talented playmakers, but its offense hasn't consistently put them in positions to succeed. Against Dallas, the combination of Irving's rushing ability, Daniels' mobility and selective downfield passing produced the team's most effective offensive showing of the season.

One game doesn't erase the problems that contributed to an 0-4 start, and Dallas entered the matchup with significant defensive struggles of its own. Still, the Buccaneers showed they don't need Daniels to throw for 300 yards to win football games. If Tampa Bay can continue to run the ball effectively, protect its young quarterback, and create manageable situations, Thursday's performance offers a blueprint worth following.

This article originally appeared on Bucs Wire: The Buccaneers may have found their offensive identity against Dallas

title: Texans report card: Grading Houston's 26-3 win over the Tennessee Titans
description: The Texans picked up their first win of the season Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. Grading Houston's performance in a 26-3 win.
fullText:
Houston Texans fans can finally breathe.

The Texans dominated the Titans defensively in a 26-3 win, earning their first victory of the season after losing their first four games.

Here are the grades from the performance:

C.J. Stroud had another efficient game, completing 26 of 34 passes for 261 yards and a touchdown. He also rushed for a 2-yard touchdown in the third quarter. Stroud is playing his best football this season, making great decisions and putting the Texans in a good position to score despite not having a running game. He's also making some clutch throws on third down.

Houston's offense had just one three-and-out, which came with six minutes remaining.

The Texans still haven't been able to get much from their running game largely because of their blocking. Several runs were also called back for holding penalties, including a would-be 24-yard touchdown. So it's impossible to put all the blame on the running backs. Woody Marks finished with 62 yards on 15 carries.

David Montogmery, who had 11 yards on five carries, injured his groin in the first half and didn't return.

It was a solid game from the wide receivers with the exception of a couple of drops. It was a blanched performance. Xavier Hutchinson led all receivers with 65 yards, followed by Nico Collins who had 56 yards. Jaylin Noel added 41 yards and a touchdown.

The offensive line gets a C because there were too many negative runs, including several penalties that negated big gains. For the most part, they were able to protect Stroud, who carved up the secondary for another good passing performance.

The defensive line got after Cam Ward in the second half. Will Anderson Jr. had three sacks, and Danielle Hunter had another. Defensive tackles Logan Hall and Sheldon Rankins both were able to get pressure on Ward. In addition, the Titans run game was inefficient. Dominique Robinson also forced a fumble

This was one of the better days for the linebackers. Azeez Al-Shaair returned after a one-game absence with a groin injury. He was all over the field. And Jake Hansen recorded his first career interception. The interception was just the second of the season for the Texans, and the second of two takeaways.

After such a poor performance in last week's loss to Dallas, one must give the Texans' secondary credit. Ward finished with less than 200 yards passing and didn't have a single touchdown. Kamari Lassiter and Derek Stingley both played well and didn't give up many explosive plays. Reed Blankenship tackled well. Unfortunately, Jalen Pitre suffered a shoulder injury that knocked him out of the game.

The special teams unit has been one of the weaknesses of this team, especially in kick return coverage.

But they were one of the most valuable units Sunday. Ka'imi Fairbairn made all four of his field goal attempts. Kai Kroeger punted it well. And the kick return defense held the Titans in check.

The penalties are a problem. The Texans were called for 11 penalties for 95 yards, often negating several positive plays, including a touchdown.

But overall it was a balanced performance from all of the Texans units, and it's why they were able to win in such decisive fashion.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle.

title: Kevon Looney: Lakers have the 'utmost confidence' in Luka Doncic
description: New Lakers center Kevon Looney says that Luka Doncic has instilled the team with a high level of belief.
fullText:
Kevon Looney is an addition to the Los Angeles Lakers' roster who may not be exciting, but he will play a key role in backing up center Walker Kessler. He is going into his 12th season in the NBA and has always been an effective and tenacious rebounder, and his experience playing on three championship teams with the Golden State Warriors will come in handy.

He knows a thing or two about playing alongside superstars, as he spent 10 seasons with Stephen Curry in Golden State, as well as three seasons as teammates with Kevin Durant there. Looney is now teamed up with Luka Doncic in L.A., and he has witnessed Doncic's improved leadership.

He talked about how Doncic leads by example and how he's instilling confidence in the rest of the Lakers following Saturday's practice session.

"When you got a guy like Luka going into the game, you feel like you can beat anybody," Looney said. "He's gonna be the best player on the court probably every night that we're out there and we feel like if we do our job, he's gonna do his job and he's gonna finish the game. He's one of the best closers in the league, so we have the utmost confidence in him and we're trying to earn his trust so he has the confidence in us as well. It makes our job a lot easier when you know you got the best player on the floor."

Doncic averaged 33.5 points, 7.7 rebounds, 8.3 assists and 1.6 steals a game and won his second scoring title last season. Just as he did during the 2025 offseason, he got into fantastic shape this offseason, and he seems poised for another monster year.

There has been talk that Looney, who is 30 years of age, is well past his prime and won't be a factor for Los Angeles this season. But he has worked the boards well in the team's three preseason games so far this month. He had nine rebounds in 18 minutes in its first game on Monday, a 127-103 win over the Sacramento Kings, and he obtained five rebounds in 17 minutes on Thursday in another win against the Kings.

title: Russian gymnasts still waiting for visas for world championships
description: Less than a week before the world gymnastics championships begin, Russia is still waiting for its visas needed to enter the Netherlands.
fullText:
Less than a week before the world gymnastics championships begin, Russia is still waiting for its visas needed to enter the Netherlands.

The Russians were supposed to leave for Rotterdam, the Netherlands, this weekend. But they pushed their departure back because they have not received visas from the Dutch government. The world championships begin Saturday, Oct. 17 with men's qualifying.

"The dates have shifted slightly," reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova said Saturday, Oct. 10, on her Telegram channel. "However, there is still plenty of time before the start, and we continue to train."

Russia faced a similar situation ahead of the European championships in Zagreb, Croatia in August. Nine members of the 65-person delegation, including Melnikova and fellow Tokyo Olympics gold medalist Viktoria Listunova, were initially denied visas. Most eventually received them, though Listunova did not.

The Russian women won the team title at Europeans with the men taking silver, and Melnikova and Anna Kalmykova went 1-2 in the all-around.

The uncertainty over Russia's visas shows how fraught the issue of its participation remains, more than four years after its athletes were largely banished from international sports in response to its unprovoked invasion of Ukraine. Though individual, neutral athletes have been allowed to compete since 2024, Russia could not send full teams to events until the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its suspension in July.

The gymnastics world championships are the first major international event where the Russians have a full team. Russia sent full teams to the world championships for fencing, modern pentathlon and rhythmic gymnastics this summer, but none of those sports are as prominent as gymnastics.

Even if Russia makes it to Rotterdam, it will not be allowed to wear its flag or colors and will be called "WG2" in deference to the Dutch government, an ally of Ukraine.

These gymnastics world championships are the first opportunity countries have to qualify for LA28, with the top three getting spots at the Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. The Russian women are expected to be the biggest challenge to the U.S. women for the team title, with the Russian men also being a medal contender.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Russian gymnasts still waiting for visas for world championships

title: Multi-agent harnesses need separate message channels
description: Today every message lands in one chat box. Upstream, downstream, sideways, peers and alerts each need their own channel.
fullText:
Today every message lands in one chat box. Upstream, downstream, sideways, peers and alerts each need their own channel.

Lately I've been wiring agents together using the same harnesses I use every day. One agent plans, a few others execute, one reviews, and I sit somewhere in the middle nudging things along. It works. It also gets confusing fast, and the models aren't the ones getting confused. I am.

Every message lands in the same chat box. A request from me, a status update from a sub-agent, a "please clarify" from the agent supervising this one, a note from a sibling agent, and a CI failure all look the same: a line of text in one long scroll. After twenty minutes I can't tell who asked for what. The agent can, since it has the whole context and can work out who said what. But I'm the one supervising this, and I end up reconstructing it by hand.

One fix is to have the agent build me a picture, using tools to draw who sent what to whom. That works, but it's a patch on top of the mess. The cleaner fix is to never mix the streams in the first place. Give each kind of communication its own channel, one I can read and audit on its own.

Today's harnesses assume a single conversation: one human talking to one agent. Once agents talk to each other, that breaks. An agent in the middle of a team actually has five streams going at once:

The easiest pair to blur is upstream and sideways, since both can be a human giving direction. The difference is where they stand. Upstream stands outside the work and talks about it: goals, deadlines, sign-off. Sideways stands inside the work and talks in it: this line, this function, this paragraph. A supervisor asks "is the login flow done?" A co-worker says "that redirect is wrong, use the callback URL." The same person can play both roles, but any single message is one or the other.

These carry different authority, different urgency, and different expectations about a reply. Squashing all five into one stream is like running your whole job out of a single email thread with your manager, your reports, your cofounder, your teammates, and your pager all on it.

The first four can be patched, uncleanly. Tag each message with its sender, add a marker for "this came from my owner," prefix alerts with [ALERT], and the agent will mostly sort it out. The last two can't be patched that way, because they're about the human, not the agent. There are just too many messages arriving too fast, and anyone trying to step in or look back gets lost in the scroll. Tags don't help me if I still have to read a thousand tagged lines to find the one that matters.

A smarter model won't fix this. The harness needs structure:

We already do this everywhere else. Org charts have had it forever. Email has To, CC, and the boss's name in the header. Slack keeps DMs apart from channels, and nobody confuses a PagerDuty page with a message from their manager. We're building multi-agent systems on a chat UI that assumed a team of one.

Single-agent harnesses got good enough that people started chaining them. The chain is becoming the unit of work, and the chat box doesn't scale with it. I want the next harness I use to make it obvious, to the agent and to me, who is talking, and whether anyone is talking at all.

Upstream, downstream, sideways, peers, alerts. Five conversations in one context. I'd switch harnesses for that alone.

Do you run multiple agents together? Do you want to manage them across vendors, harnesses, and machines, all from one place? Do you want to do it from any browser and your phone? Try reminal.

title: Impersonating Grok Bot for Fun and (No) Profit
description: How I forged Grok Bot's Web Bot Auth signatures and used them to scrape sites behind Cloudflare.
fullText:
A few months ago on August 11, 2026 SpaceXAI released an AI personal assistant named Grok Bot. According to Cloudflare Radar and browsing X it seems like it has been quite successful. However, while playing around with Grok Bot I noticed many odd things. One thing in particular drew my attention. While looking at requests in Chrome’s DevTools I noticed three headers used to cryptographically sign requests, Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent. I immediately recognized this is Web Bot Auth (WBA) and wondered how it was injected.

Web Bot Auth is a standard that verifies the identity of an automated bot such as AI agents by using Signature headers. Instead of relying on the User-Agent or IP allowlists, it requires bot operators to cryptographically sign their requests using a private key and publishing the corresponding public key (JWK) on their domain at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory. This allows site operators to prove a bot’s identity. You can find more details at Cloudflare’s Web Bot Auth documentation and their announcement post in partnership with Browserbase, a data acquisition company.

After creating a Bot and opening its desktop environment, I started digging around and I found a file of interest at /usr/local/bin/sand-web-bot-auth.mjs. This file is also contained in a package that can be directly downloaded from their CDN here. It appears to make a few calls to Cursor’s API to get the signing data and then inject them into Chrome via Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP):

Alright, but how do we get an auth token to call the API with? My first instinct was to run printenv. However, it didn’t contain the token. This is because in /usr/local/bin/start-exec-daemon they run:

This deletes the required token from the environment. However, the sand-web-bot-auth.mjs still needs the token to run. You can get the token by getting the process ID and then dumping the process environment variables:

And just like that, you have your very own SAND_INFERENCE_RENEWAL_CREDENTIAL. Now you can forge your very own Grok Bot signature headers with:

The signature is valid for 90 seconds despite the API stating cacheTtlSeconds: 30 seconds.

Normally when you ask an agent to request a page it will make a tool call to that agent provider’s backend and sign the request as it’s making it. This way you have no control over the signing process. But here you have control of the Docker container which requests the signing signatures. This undermines the authenticity of the Web Bot Auth signatures since anyone can request a signing signature for any site and impersonate Grok Bot.

Instead, Grok Bot’s backend should MITM traffic from outside the Docker container. This way the user has no control over the signing process. This also has the benefit of signing curl traffic from the terminal, not just Chrome. A more temporary fix could be restricting what IPs can invoke the signing endpoints to only the ranges of the AWS IPs Grok Bot runs.

Unrelated, but of note, if you look through the Docker container you’ll begin to notice there are many ways to detect Grok Bot as a website operator. For example, they don’t do enough patching of the browser environment and this often results in an infinite loop when met with a managed Cloudflare challenge.

Some sites could potentially allowlist Grok Bot, but I see that as unlikely. In that case, you might be able to bypass their WAFs such as Cloudflare (5-second challenge). However, starting September 15th 2026, Cloudflare will allow AI crawlers by default. You could use the impersonated signature headers to scrape sites and bypass Cloudflare while pretending to be Grok Bot. I believe this can affect most sites protected by Cloudflare since default settings are powerful and not likely to be changed. However, it won’t affect sites that explicitly request a managed challenge for example via Security Rules or disallow agents.

Below is a practical demonstration of this. On the left, a site is accessed through a suspicious IP and is blocked by Cloudflare (Just a moment...). On the right, that same site is accessed using that same suspicious IP but with forged Grok Bot Web Bot Auth signature headers, which is successful.

title: Your IP Has Been Reset
fullText:
Much of the Western world’s economy is founded on the idea that knowledge work carries incredible value. This could be in the form of our designs, our rare knowledge, time-tested processes, or the novel materials that we develop.

Intellectual property law exists to protect the value of this work; nobody else may steal what we have spent our precious resources to create. Its scarcity begets its value. We’ve all grown up in a world where IP lawsuits are to be taken very seriously.

The barrier to entry used to be money: money which bought you people’s time, effort and talent in many forms. It wasn’t an efficient business (see: the end of organisations). Much of an organisation’s resources go into the business of simply running it.

People practically everywhere have rightly spent the last few years complaining about the global-scale IP theft that has fuelled our current LLM boom. The lawsuits which followed came predictably too late, and were reduced to restitution that looks paltry next to the valuations it was paid out of. They already got away with it.

Even worse, it was discovered that AI companies had been buying up millions of physical books, slicing off their spines and scanning them for training data, before unceremoniously dispatching them off to be pulped.

IP used to be safeguarded within an organisation. The world outside couldn’t access its hard-won treasures. And over the years, we were forced to pay an increasingly hefty price for the access we’d come to rely upon. Cory Doctorow’s term “enshittification” caught the public imagination as this pattern writ large, and consumer resentment began to foment.

But now, with AI, the value of all prior knowledge work is rapidly plummeting to zero. Today’s models are fully capable of decompiling, understanding and recomposing software. You can now generate new proposals, whether for drug trials, legal contracts or product designs.

Hell, OpenAI just released 722 new maths papers. On a Tuesday.

Already, one developer has rebuilt the bloated and overpriced Adobe suite and given it away for free. Others have decompiled classic console games to run in a web browser, and are now recombining them into custom mash-ups, for the sheer fun of it.

Perhaps it’s time for Revenge of the Nerds: “They enjoyed screwing us over—now it’s our turn to do the same.”

With the walls of IP (slowly and quietly) collapsing all around us, it seems we may all be headed back to square one.

title: Why demand for the shingles vaccine is soaring
description: Could a drug intended to prevent painful rashes also protect our brains as we get older? The signs are promising – but not conclusive. Yet that’s enough to be driving a boom in shingles jabs
fullText:
Could a drug intended to prevent painful rashes also protect our brains as we get older? The signs are promising – but not conclusive. Yet that’s enough to be driving a boom in shingles jabs

When Jenny, a 50-year-old marketing and branding professional from Cambridge, went for her shingles vaccine last year, an entirely different disease was on her mind. Having witnessed three of her four grandparents succumb to dementia, with all the distress that brought, she wants to avoid the same fate. She hopes the shingles vaccine might help.

Jenny is far from alone. Britain’s high street chemists have reported a rise in demand for the shingles vaccine, at least some of which is driven by people more worried about dementia than shingles. And while the vaccine is free for some on the NHS, most under-65s pay around £450 for the full two doses.

The trend follows a flurry of studies that suggest, but do not prove, that the shingles vaccination might offer some protection against dementia. How much protection? It depends on how the study is done, but scientists have reported as much as a 20% reduction in risk, with the strongest effects in women. On a brutal disease that has no cure, the impact could be profound. “Imagine a vaccine that became a medicine for dementia,” says John Todd, professor of precision medicine at the University of Oxford and one of the scientists involved. “Wow. Wouldn’t that be amazing?”

Recent figures from Boots show that bookings for its shingles vaccination service more than doubled over the past year, after rising 30% in the year before. A similar trend has played out at Superdrug, where bookings are up 41% year on year.

Of course, many who go for their shots simply want to avoid shingles. It’s a painful rash, triggered by reactivation of the chickenpox virus which lies dormant in the nervous system after a childhood infection. The vaccine is not approved for any other condition. But dozens of people who contacted the Guardian said preventing dementia was at least part of their reason for getting the shots.

“I want to feel as if I’ve done everything I can to try to head it off, in terms of risk factors and preventive measures that are available to me now,” says Jenny. “If there’s a potential for this to give me more time without the onset of dementia in 20 years’ time, then God, I’ll take it.”

Nearly 60 million people live with dementia globally, but the figure is set to rise with population growth and ageing. By 2040, more than 100 million people are projected to have the disease. In England and Wales, it’s expected dementia could affect 1.7 million people that year, with the annual cost reaching £90bn.

The most common form of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, is associated with the abnormal buildup of proteins in the brain. Plaques (clusters) of amyloid accumulate between neurons, and tangles of another protein, tau, form inside the nerve cells. New drugs can clear amyloid plaques and slow the disease, but so far the impact on patients appears small and the side-effects can be serious.

The wave of work on the shingles vaccine was spurred by suspicions that the virus that causes chickenpox and shingles, varicella zoster virus or VZV, might somehow contribute to dementia. After a chickenpox infection, some virus remains in the body, lying dormant in neurons. As the immune system weakens with age, or is suppressed through medications or stress, the virus can reactivate and travel down nerve cells to the skin where it causes shingles. In the brain, the virus can drive inflammation, nerve cell stress and the accumulation of amyloid and tau.

In an influential paper in Nature last year, researchers at Stanford University in California focused on a natural experiment that arose in Wales during a shingles vaccination programme. The vaccine on offer, Zostavax, was a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning it contained a weakened version of the varicella zoster virus. It was made available from 1 September 2013, but anyone who was 80 or older on that day was ineligible, because it becomes less effective the older a person gets.

The age-related cutoff split the older population into two groups: those who could get the vaccine and those who could not. This allowed scientists to compare dementia rates in thousands of people born on different sides of the eligibility line.

When the Stanford team ran the numbers, they found that dementia rates were 8.5% lower in the vaccine-eligible group over seven years, in women, but not in men (the gender disparity in this experiment remains unexplained). Since only about half of the group went along for their shots, the researchers concluded that the vaccine lowered dementia risk by nearly 20%. They have since reported similar effects in Australia and Ontario, Canada.

“We have a really compelling body of data from these studies,” says Pascal Geldsetzer, an epidemiologist on the Stanford studies. “We’re much more confident that what we’re looking at is cause and effect rather than just correlation.”

More evidence came in 2024 from the University of Oxford, when Todd teamed up with psychiatrists Maxime Taquet and Paul Harrison to study Shingrix, a newer and more potent shingles vaccine that has largely replaced Zostavax. Shingrix is not a live-attenuated vaccine but contains viral proteins and an adjuvant – an additive designed to strengthen the body’s immune response and so make the vaccine more effective. In this case, the adjuvant is made of tiny fat-based particles called liposomes that are filled with various compounds that stimulate different parts of the immune response.

The Oxford team analysed health records for more than 200,000 US citizens who were vaccinated for shingles. About half had Shingrix and half Zostavax. Over the next six years, dementia cases were 17% lower in those who had Shingrix compared with Zostavax, amounting to an extra 164 days lived without the condition. Women fared better, with a 22% lower risk compared with 13% for men. (Women have a higher dementia risk, which seems mostly down to them living longer.) One benefit of the study was that it compared Zostavax v Shingrix rather than vaccinated v unvaccinated people. That reduced the risk of the results being skewed by the “health vaccinee” bias, whereby people who get vaccinated are generally more health conscious and do more to reduce their risk of dementia in other ways.

“I thought wow, I’ll just book the vaccine online,” says Todd. “If by chance it does lower the risk of dementia, I’m 68 – why wouldn’t I take that? And also, it’s really effective against shingles.” Todd is a consultant for GSK, the manufacturer of Shingrix, but the company had no involvement in any of the studies.

More recent work hints at other potential benefits of the vaccine. In August, the Oxford team published a paper showing a reduced risk of heart attacks and stroke after the Shingrix vaccination. The effect is small, but across the population it could prevent thousands of deaths per year. Separate work at Kaiser Permanente, the US healthcare giant, found a similar effect.

The results are exciting, but none of this is proof. Critical questions remain. In July, researchers at the University of Bristol, and others including Geldsetzer, found no evidence in much larger English hospital records that Zostavax protects against dementia. That may be due to quirks in the data or how it is analysed, or a sign that the old Zostavax vaccine does not protect against dementia after all. Geldsetzer suspects hospital data is not the best for studying dementia, as most patients are managed in primary care.

Precisely how the vaccine might protect against dementia is still a puzzle. By stimulating the immune system to attack VZV, the vaccine might help to reduce inflammation and cellular damage in the brain. There may be knock-on effects whereby inflammation reactivates another dormant virus, the cold sore-causing HSV1, which in turn drives Alzheimer’s-like damage. The vaccine may also have broader effects, boosting ailing immune systems so they are better at clearing harmful waste from the brain.

One avenue scientists are exploring is whether the adjuvant, which is in Shingrix but not Zostavax, is important for protection against dementia. The Oxford team suspect that might explain why a vaccine for respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, which contains the same adjuvant as Shingrix, also appears to protect against dementia. The adjuvant specifically stimulates T-cells that are central to the immune response to the virus. “You want a really healthy immune system to do the garbage collection of damaged neurons,” says Todd.

The lack of hard proof hasn’t stopped people taking action. Jenny had already had a bout of shingles – “It looked like I’d been slapped across the face by a zombie,” she says – but it was the fear of dementia that prompted her to get vaccinated. She made the decision after reading the research for herself, wary that the press might have hyped it.

Sally, a 68-year-old former headteacher in Telford, Shropshire, cared for her mother with dementia for five years. “It does bring you up very sharply when you’re considering your own future,” she says. Sally runs marathons, watches her nutrition carefully and does all she can to protect herself from the disease. “I was going to have the shingles jab anyway, but when I saw the research saying there may be a protective effect against dementia, I jumped at it. The experience of caring for someone who developed dementia was pivotal in my decision.” She got the jabs on the NHS.

It could be a while before we have clear answers. Todd and colleagues want to do a mechanistic study to understand at the deepest level what happens to the immune system when people have the shingles vaccination. Meanwhile, two major clinical trials are under way in Finland and Denmark to see whether Shingrix genuinely protects against dementia, but they won’t report for years.

What should people do in the meantime? Geldsetzer says that while vaccine recommendations are a matter for government advisory bodies, he wouldn’t discourage people who want to get the shingles vaccine for dementia protection. Todd says: “I have been suggesting to friends and colleagues to get the vaccine if they are 50 or over – it’s safe.”

Alzheimer’s Research UK does not advise people to have the shingles vaccine specifically to prevent dementia. Instead, it recommends all the healthy habits we know promote brain health: exercise, a good diet and challenging the brain throughout life. Michael Jones, evidence manager at the charity, says: “While new studies finding these links are promising and growing in number, there isn’t enough data to demonstrate a direct cause-and-effect relationship.”

Dominic, a 61-year-old engineer in Christchurch, Dorset, paid for the Shingrix vaccine last year. His father had shingles, the classic rash around the torso, which lasted for months. His eldest sister had shingles, too. It affected her eye and caused minor damage. A cousin also developed the condition. Dominic planned to get the shot, but only acted after reading the dementia research. “I really don’t want to get shingles,” he says. “That could strike at anytime. And when does dementia start? We just don’t know, do we?”

title: Doiter – Language where pointers and stack frames are Docker containers
description: A cloud-native programming language which uses docker as virtual memory by representing pointers as docker containers, and fields as files. - simvux/doiter
fullText:
Doiter uses the running docker daemon as it's virtual memory. It does so by creating a docker container for each allocation/stack-frame. Each structure will also be allocated as a nullable pointer. So taking the following example:

The following containers will be created

There's two primitive types and literals, byte and char.
For conditionals, there's the when statement. See samples/hello-world.dr for details.

The compiler does have error messages with line spans to help you create your own monsters. Enjoy!

Should I use Doiter?

No. This is a terrible idea on every level.

Is this project vibe-coded?

No. Zero AI was used in the making of this monstrosity.

Why? 

This project was created as a submission to a hackathon where the goal was to create a "spooky" programming language during October.

I decided that sufficiently cursed would count as spooky.

How good is the performance?

Currently samples/hello-world.dr takes about a minute to run on my machine. With the state of the industry, this isn't too bad in comparison.

As there are no strings/arrays it's implemented with a linked list. This means that each character of "Hello World" gets its own docker container. In total it spawns 51 docker containers.

Woah you must love docker?

No. This project is a parody of unnecessary docker use and overabstraction.

Does Doiter use Garbage Collection?

Doiter uses missile allocation. Meaning that no docker containers are cleaned up during execution but all docker containers are automatically removed when the program has completed.

Are you also working on a real programming language?

Yes. Check out luminalang/lumina.

title: World Bank chief warns diesel, fertilizer and El Niño pressures are building at once
description:
Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth. 
   The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held ‌outside of Washington for the first time in three years. 
   IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters during a tour of the 300,000 square-meter Queen Sirikit National Convention Center on Sunday evening that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the ‌last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023. 
   SEVERAL FINANCE MINISTERS STAYING AWAY 
   Notably absent will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16.
fullText:
BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.

The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held ‌outside of Washington for the first time in three years.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters during a tour of the 300,000 square-meter Queen Sirikit National Convention Center on Sunday evening that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the ‌last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023.

SEVERAL FINANCE MINISTERS STAYING AWAY

Notably absent will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16.

Several other ​finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said.

Bessent's decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the U.S. leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine's battle against Russia's invasion and the U.S. move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.

World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world's oil, pressures were building again. Soaring prices for diesel, rising fertilizer prices and a looming "super" El Niño weather effect that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are all hitting at once.

Group of Seven countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, ‌who is keen to see lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party ⁠lose control of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of U.S. sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.

More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the amount of ⁠oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices.

Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it's the combination ... What's happening to fertilizer prices? What's happening to energy costs? What's happening to debt? It's that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months."

IMF chief Georgieva issued a similar warning in ​her ​traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings last week, telling the audience: "Winter is coming."

The IMF has signaled little change in its forecast for 3% global growth in 2026 and ​may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in ‌its fifth year of war against Russia's invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.

IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.

One huge headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030.

Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.

Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400 billion in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue on average.

Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt ‌service payments for the poorest countries, but there is little appetite for such action now, according to diplomats from G20 countries, who said high debt levels and political ​pressures posed bigger hurdles this time.

Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper reforms as a condition for approving ​lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.

"Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going ​high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse."

Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting ‌public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young.

The IMF ​risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many ​developing countries.

"As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said.

Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to global travelers descending on Thailand's bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent attacks on Saudi airports.

The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people in Israel, followed by Israel's bombardment of Gaza that killed more than ​74,000 people and devastated cities throughout the Palestinian area.

Three years later, the linkage between national security and international finance ‌is clear, although finance officials at the time had dismissed the Hamas attack as not being an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council.

"Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we're currently experiencing ​with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago."

Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive ​and they have to recognize that they don't live in the world they used to."

title: Arizona's GOP keeps embracing election deniers who lose. It could happen again.
description:

fullText:
Election Day 2020 was fast approaching, and Alexander Kolodin wanted a spot inside the Arizona Republican Party's war room.

Kolodin, an attorney who had lost a GOP primary for the state Senate that summer, was seen as something of a gadfly by some in the state GOP and hardly seen at all by others. But the Republicans running the show allowed him into an auxiliary war room on another floor of the hotel, distanced from the real action, one party leader recalled. People there "could say they were in the war room," he said. "If we needed something, then we'd call."

Kolodin didn't wait to be summoned. On Election Day, complaints began flooding in about ballots marked with Sharpie markers. Soon, supporters of President Donald Trump were blaming Sharpies for what looked like a loss in Arizona.

The Arizona Republican Party had investigated the matter and determined that Sharpies had not in fact caused problems. So its leaders were surprised when they learned that Kolodin was filing a lawsuit demanding that voters who used Sharpies be given a chance to vote again.

The suit was filed the day after the election, the first of several challenges Kolodin championed over the 2020 results. Each failed in court, and they led to sanctions from the state bar association. But Kolodin's embrace of these claims catapulted him from a little-known attorney who badly lost his first campaign for office to a leading figure in Arizona politics and this year's Republican nominee for secretary of state.

If he wins, he will be responsible for running the state's elections in 2028, when Arizona is expected to once again be a battleground in the presidential and Senate contests. Other election conspiracy theorists hold high office, but a victory here would mark the first time someone actively involved in attempting to subvert election results would be elected to run a state's elections.

Arizona was a reliably Republican state just a decade ago, and then seen as a competitive battleground. But in recent years, the state GOP has repeatedly nominated candidates who have promoted Trump's false claims, only to see them lose in the general election. That includes Blake Master, who lost a Senate race in 2022, and Kari Lake, who lost races for governor in 2022 and Senate in 2024, even as Trump won the state.

This fall, besides Kolodin, two other Republicans who acted to subvert the 2020 election results are also on the ballot: Andy Biggs for governor and Warren Petersen for attorney general.

Some in the party predict a wipeout is coming and worry Democrats will consolidate and expand their power for years to come if Republicans continue this pattern.

"The election denialists have dominated this party for six years," said one GOP strategist. "If we keep doing this, we will keep losing."

Kolodin is not the only person who has advanced the lie that the 2020 election was stolen and is now running to oversee elections in a presidential battleground state. In Nevada, former state lawmaker Jim Marchant, the GOP nominee for secretary of state, claimed that both he and Trump were victims of election fraud in 2020 and says being called an election denier is a "badge of honor." In a recent interview, Anthony Forlini, Michigan's GOP nominee for secretary of state, wouldn't say who won the presidential election in 2020. "Everyone wants to trip up people on that whole question," he said.

In Arizona, endorsing and promoting Trump's conspiracy theories were essential to Kolodin's rise. They brought him to the center of the action, drew admirers in the GOP base and won allies in powerful places.

"Alex definitely stepped up when there were very few who could or would," said Tyler Bowyer, CEO of Turning Point USA. "He easily could have been, 'Nah, I'm not going to help.' No one would know who he was and he certainly wouldn't be running for secretary of state now."

The cases increased Kolodin's public profile, but it came with a price, said Tyler Montague, president of the Arizona Public Integrity Alliance, a conservative think tank, who has known Kolodin for more than a decade and sometimes worked with him.

"He found a path to notoriety and surrendered some of his political thinking to Trump, and that combination led him to where he's at," he said. "It's a cultlike mentality - uncritical acceptance of what the leader says. It's hard for him to get out of it because it's also the source of his status."

After fighting for Trump following his 2020 loss, Kolodin was elected to the Arizona House in 2022. There, he earned a reputation as a fighter for ultraconservative principles, but also as an obstructionist who has incensed fellow Republicans as well as Democrats. Two GOP committee chairmen asked for him to be removed from their committees, three people familiar with the situation said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss a personnel matter.

Kolodin did not respond to requests for comment or to a list of detailed questions.

In other interviews, he has emphasized his support for election integrity, attacked his opponent's record and tried to downplay the events of 2020.

"Election integrity has become the defining civil rights issue of our time," he wrote in a post on X thanking Trump for his endorsement. "We must protect the sanctity of every lawful vote, and we must restore confidence in our elections for every lawful voter, regardless of political party."

Kolodin was raised in Arizona and returned to the state after earning a law degree at the University of Pennsylvania in 2013. He set up his own small law practice, taking a series of cases where he challenged government and election procedures, often on hot-button topics of public interest that landed in the news.

Among them: He demanded public records in a sports arena deal. He tried to kill mask requirements in a public school district during the pandemic. And he worked to kick a congressional candidate off the ballot because of an error on her nominating petitions.

Kolodin made his first run for political office in 2020, mounting a mostly self-funded primary campaign against a Republican incumbent for a state Senate seat. During that campaign, his opponent latched on to Kolodin's involvement in a 2014 defamation lawsuit where he represented a liberal activist who had collected and mailed a huge pile of filled-out ballots. Kolodin lost the case, and also badly lost the GOP primary.

But he continued his work on election issues. That fall, he scored a victory in a dispute with Adrian Fontes, who at the time was running elections in Maricopa County, home to Phoenix and the state's largest county. Fontes had told voters that if they made a mistake marking their ballot, they could cross it out and fill in the proper oval. Kolodin's suit argued that this would open the door to allowing people who handle ballots to change votes after the fact. His suit forced a reversal by Fontes, a Democrat who is the current secretary of state and Kolodin's opponent this fall.

But when Election Day arrived, his profile began to climb with his Sharpie lawsuit. The allegations, first voiced in remote corners of Twitter, were soon amplified by conservative mega-voices such as Charlie Kirk of Turning Point USA. By 10 a.m. the next day, there were 1,200 tweets per minute on Sharpies, one analysis found.

Kolodin asked Montague, the conservative think tank president, if he would be a plaintiff in his Sharpie suit, Montague said. He declined, telling Kolodin there was nothing to these claims. The rumor was based on concerns that using a Sharpie marker would invalidate a ballot because the ink could bleed through and interfere with ballot marks on the other side of the paper. In fact, as the state GOP had discovered, the columns on the other side of the paper were aligned so that any bleed through would not impact other votes.

Nonetheless, Kolodin "charged forward," Montague recalled. "He seemed to genuinely believe in the various conspiracy theories going on."

One Republican attorney active in the party said Kolodin pursued the suit despite widespread opposition among Republican strategists in D.C. and Arizona. "It felt like he was trying to elbow his way into the conversation and, frankly, the limelight," he said.

The case was quickly dismissed, but within weeks, Kolodin was back with another, more sweeping lawsuit, demanding that the election results be set aside due to "massive election fraud."

The suit - one of several filed in states Joe Biden won - was conceived by national figures including Trump ally Sidney Powell, who promised these challenges would "release the kraken" and prove Trump actually won the election. She needed an attorney to carry the case, but no prominent Arizona election lawyer, including those who had worked for the Trump campaign and the Republican Party, would take the case, said three people familiar with the conversations inside GOP circles. Kolodin stepped in.

"Most of the Republican attorneys saw the need to be as far away from this dumpster fire as you could possible get," said one of these people. "Were you to continue to pursue these cases you could be jeopardizing your law license."

A federal judge found the allegations "sorely wanting of relevant or reliable evidence" and in December 2020, dismissed the case.

Despite the courtroom setbacks, Kolodin was establishing himself as Arizona's go-to attorney when someone wanted to challenge election results. He represented Cyber Ninjas, which in 2021 ran a chaotic audit of 2020 ballots in Maricopa County (and ultimately found Biden's margin slightly bigger than official results indicated). In 2022, he represented a group that monitored ballot drop boxes and filmed people voting, claiming to be hunting for fraud. And his client list included people who falsely presented themselves as 2020 electors.

In 2023, the State Bar of Arizona cited three lawsuits Kolodin filed, including the Sharpie suit, as it formally admonished him for violating his duty to the legal profession, the legal system and the public. The state bar sentenced him to 18 months of probation and required him to take five legal ethics courses.

But while Kolodin was accumulating one loss after the next, his public profile was rising. In 2022, he again ran for the legislature, seeking a House seat representing Scottsdale, a suburb of Phoenix. His campaign material highlighted his role in many of these actions.

And unlike in summer 2020, this time he won.

Kolodin immediately made his mark in the Capitol, irritating people in both parties with unpredictable personal and legislative behavior, according to current and former lawmakers and others familiar with the situation.

He became known for filing voluminous numbers of bills - 74 last year - and also for a proposal last year that would bar any legislator from introducing more than 10 bills per year. He backed a repeal of the ban on machine guns, silencers, sawed-off shotguns and pipe bombs. He was the only legislator of either party to vote against a "stolen valor" bill making it a crime to impersonate a veteran. (He said it would criminalize alleged lies by politicians, setting a dangerous precedent.)

Several current and former GOP lawmakers described him as disruptive, unwilling to work with others and insistent on having things his way. Last year, he called any legislator, including some Republicans, who supported a particular version of a budget bill "an enemy of the people of Arizona."

"He says things out loud that are nonsensical - objecting to motions, attempting to change procedure in a nonsensical way, outbursts in a heated debate on the floor," said one Republican who worked closely with Kolodin. His style, he said, is to "fly off the handle" and "shoot from the hip."

On the campaign trail, Kolodin touts bipartisan successes, and in 2024, he helped reach a bipartisan elections reform package, which aligned post-election timelines for steps such as certification with new federal deadlines.

But last year, he blew up chances for a bipartisan agreement with Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs's office on another elections measure by insisting on elements that the governor would never agree to - such as requirements making mail voting harder - and being unwilling to compromise, according to two people involved in the process.

"He has particular views on certain issues and it's challenging to reason with him or find common ground," said Bo Dul, an Arizona election attorney who served as general counsel to Hobbs. "Often, those views are not grounded in fact or how election administration actually works and, as a result, he would often insist on positions that are just nonstarters."

No deal was reached. Instead, the GOP legislature voted to put its proposal before voters this fall. If approved, it would, among other things, require mail-in voters - who make up about 80 percent of all voters in the state - to show identification. It's unclear how or where people voting by mail would be able to show ID.

Kolodin has bemoaned failure to advance another election priority: requiring every voter to repeatedly verify their address to vote by mail. In an interview last year, he said that this reform could have helped increase Republican vote share in Arizona.

"It could have flipped this state red for a generation. So I was just so incredibly disappointed to see it get killed," he told "The Jeff Oravits Show."

Kolodin's panache for irritating his party and for advancing Trump's unfounded claims collided when a group of Arizona Republicans was criminally investigated, and then charged with conspiracy and fraud, for declaring themselves to be the state's representatives to the electoral college in 2020 when Biden actually won Arizona.

In 2024, Kolodin, who represented some of these so-called fake electors, argued that the Arizona Republican Party's insurance policy should cover some of the electors' legal fees. He wrote the company that these people were officials of the Arizona Republican Party, according to a letter viewed by The Washington Post.

The insurance company wound up paying out the policy's $1 million maximum toward their legal defense, documents show, some of which went to a law firm where Kolodin worked.

In January 2026, then-Arizona Republican Party Chairwoman Gina Swoboda informed the party's executive committee that he had done this without consulting her or other party officers and that the result was a 10-fold hike in premiums.

"We became aware of this matter in October 2025 when we inquired why our renewal premium was so high," she wrote. She said the party then made the "difficult but necessary decision" to drop coverage for 2026. That meant the officers of the party were vulnerable if they faced damages claims or lawsuits.

This summer, Kolodin easily won the GOP primary for secretary of state, beating Swoboda, who had left her position as party chair earlier this year. He is running on election integrity, promising to implement "robust security protocols" and restore confidence in the elections system.

But some in his party worry Kolodin's history of questioning election results could harm Republicans. "He is making outrageous lies about very important things related to the office that he is seeking," said Ken Bennett, a former Republican secretary of state and state senator in Arizona.

"As long as the Republican Party nominates people who are too far to the right of the mainstream ... those nominees are going to have trouble in the general election," Bennett said of Kolodin.

The events of 2020 loom large in Kolodin's race. During a spirited "candidates in conversation" on Arizona public television with his opponent, Kolodin was asked directly if he was an "election denier."

"That's absurd," he replied. "I have one of the greatest bipartisan track records of working on elections issues of anybody in recent Arizona history."

Pressed again as to whether he was an election denier, Kolodin answered, "No."

Followed by reporters into the hallway after the event, he was asked directly if Trump won Arizona in 2020.

"I think I answered that question," Kolodin replied.

Asked again, Kolodin said, "Look, Joe Biden was the president. Congress said that Joe Biden won. Congress called the race."

As for who won Arizona, Kolodin refused to say, asserting that he had already answered the question. After about a minute of this back and forth, the elevator arrived and Kolodin stepped in. Reporters kept pressing: Was the ballot count in Maricopa County accurate?

"It's time for us to go," Kolodin replied. He insisted again that he had already answered, and the elevator doors closed.

title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, but Zelensky says it's news to him
description:

fullText:
President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict. There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly said this “was news for me.”

Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to continue their aerial attacks on each other’s energy facilities.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” He did not elaborate further on what the ceasefire might include.

Zelenskyy told Axios that he knew nothing about a ceasefire deal.

“But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree,” Zelenskyy said, according to Axios. “If President Trump negotiated it with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it.”

NBC News has reached out to Zelenskyy’s office for further comment.

It follows a dramatic few days in which Trump agreed to a diesel deal with the Kremlin, demanded Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. The shift left Kyiv and its European allies reeling.

The U.S. agreed Friday to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal that Trump said would see Russia “immediately” release 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and global marketplace,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.

After strong criticism from Zelenskyy, Trump said Saturday: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals.”

Trump has sought to blame the Ukraine conflict, rather than his own assault on Iran, for a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices to record highs since the U.S. launched the Middle East war in February.

Zelenskyy reiterated Sunday that he was ready to halt strikes on Russian refineries if the Kremlin halts its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

“We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy — both sides,” he said in interview on ABC News’ “This Week.” He added that if Russia wants an energy ceasefire, “we are open for this.”

“Don’t attack us,” he said. “Don’t kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel.”

The Ukrainian president also told ABC News he would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

Zelenskyy said “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to ​change who is ​leading Ukraine.

He ⁠said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel ​prices “when everybody in the world understands [that] ​because ⁠of the war in [the] Middle East, the prices are rising.”

Zelenskyy was also asked on ABC News why Trump and Elon Musk blamed the Ukrainian president for the war’s continuation.

“Because these people can’t find a key how to stop Putin, because it’s more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others, because it’s more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine,” he responded, pointing to how the war in Iran was leading to higher fuel prices.

title: 6 senators call for White House to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
description:
— A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. 
Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.

Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.

The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.

Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.

"We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied," Tillis said.

Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.

The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.

"Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law."

Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law.

"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said on CBS's "Face the Nation."

He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.

"This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world," Barrasso said.

Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

title: ICE agent strikes man with car during pursuit in Texas, authorities say
description:
A man was hospitalized after he was struck by a vehicle driven by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who was allegedly pursuing him and another man on Saturday, Texas law enforcement officials and ICE said.
Maj. Anthony McConnell of the Harris County Sheriff's Office's Special Investigation Bureau told reporters that around 7:20 a.m. local time, law enforcement officers were called to Clay Road near Highway 6 just outside Houston after the unidentified ICE agent called 911 for an ambulance for the man, later identified by ICE as Miguel Parra-Hernandez, who was struck.
fullText:
The injured man was identified as Miguel Parra-Hernandez, officials said.

A man was hospitalized after he was struck by a vehicle driven by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who was allegedly pursuing him and another man on Saturday, Texas law enforcement officials and ICE said.

Maj. Anthony McConnell of the Harris County Sheriff's Office's Special Investigation Bureau told reporters that around 7:20 a.m. local time, law enforcement officers were called to Clay Road near Highway 6 just outside Houston after the unidentified ICE agent called 911 for an ambulance for the man, later identified by ICE as Miguel Parra-Hernandez, who was struck.

An ICE spokesperson said in a statement that the agency was attempting to arrest another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national who they allege had a criminal record and a final order of removal by a judge.

The ICE agent allegedly observed Mendoza-Cervantes and Parra-Hernandez, who the agency alleged was undocumented, enter a car and attempted a car stop, according to ICE.

McConnell said the ICE agent allegedly was pursuing the man and another person in their car and during the chase, the driver and the passenger left their vehicle on foot.

Surveillance video of the incident reviewed by ABC News appears to show the agent maneuvering his vehicle in the direction of the man running and striking him with the vehicle.

ICE alleged in a statement that "Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck."

Parra-Hernandez appeared to suffer a broken leg, McConnell said. He was taken to the hospital and is in ICE custody, according to ICE.

ICE didn't immediately list any criminal history about Parra-Hernandez.

McConnell referred further inquiries about the incident to ICE.

"We're here to investigate the crash," he told reporters.

Deputies were collecting video evidence from nearby buildings as part of their investigation, McConnell said. No arrests have been made.

Mendoza-Cervantes was not found as of Sunday afternoon, ICE said.

Family members of Parra-Hernandez, community leaders and officials of the immigration FIEL Houston held a news conference in Houston on Sunday.

"We have been in contact with Miguel’s family, and they are very worried about his health. He is alive but is supposed to undergo surgery for his leg, which is broken in three places," said Cesar Espinosa, executive director at FIEL Houston.

Espinosa demanded accountability from ICE and called for a transparent investigation of the incident.

"We have more questions than answers. The biggest question we have is why does this keep happening? We demand answers and transparency from all agencies involved," Espinosa said.

Harris County Precinct 4 Commissioner Lesley Briones called on ICE to provide all evidence to the Harris County Sheriff's office and to cooperate with the investigation, adding that she was "horrified" about the incident.

"We demand full transparency, accountability, and respect for the rule of law," she said in her statement.

Harris County Attorney Abbie Kamin said, "Time is of the essence in getting the facts, and the public deserves clear, accurate answers."

"ICE must cooperate fully with the local investigation," Kamin said. "My office supports Sheriff Ed Gonzalez and District Attorney Sean Teare in their ongoing independent investigation, and the Harris County Attorney's Office stands ready to assist and support these critical efforts. We will continue to monitor developments closely as the facts become clear."

The Texas incident comes two days after ICE agents shot a man inside his car with his 5-year-old son in the backseat in New York City during an attempted arrest.

Oscar Belgal, 28, is currently being held in custody and awaiting court appearances following the incident.

ICE alleged Belgal, a Dominican national, "weaponized his vehicle," and rammed ICE vehicles. Surveillance footage released by the police showed the initial encounter where two armed men approached Belgal's car and hit the driver side window.

Several New York City officials, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, condemned ICE's actions and called on the federal government to remove them from the city.

'Don't stop swinging' - Clonduff end 26-year wait for Down title
description: Clonduff end a 26-year wait for the Down SFC title with a 1-14 to 1-10 victory over Burren at Pairc Esler.
fullText:
Clonduff ended 26 years of hurt to finally get their hands back on the Frank O'Hare Cup with a 1-14 to 1-10 win over Burren in the Down Senior Football Championship final at Pairc Esler.

It was a cagey affair across the hour in Newry as both sides bid for county glory, Burren losing their third final in four years as Clonduff prevailed in their first decider appearance since 2016.

The Mourne county has been under the stranglehold of Kilcoo dominance for what feels like an eternity, with this final the first without the Magpies in 15 years, as their bid for eight titles in a row was halted by Burren in the last four.

As both sides looked to impose themselves, it was captain Charlie Carr's goal that gave the men in yellow an early advantage.

A couple of two-point frees from Eamon Brown ensured a 1-6 to 0-4 lead at the break, and the forward put the success down to the words of Mayo All-Ireland winning boss Andy Moran.

"I was actually listening to Andy Moran's podcast during the week, and just one thing he said, just don't stop swinging whatever happens, just keep shooting and just keep shooting," Brown told BBC Sport NI.

"It's unbelievable. The fans throughout the whole game were actually unbelievable, we had a 16th man, any time we scored, the roar was just incredible. Any time Burren made a mistake, it was our roar.

"You know, finals...you can think of the occasion or whatever, but our whole thing was, as long as we work harder than them, we want it more than them. That's what it comes down to, and that's what we've done."

Repeat pairings set for Derry and Fermanagh finals

Carr's goal was a real captain's contribution to settle any early nerves, while his composure was key as Niall Toner's 41st-minute goal threatened to stir a comeback.

"It's very hard to put into words, you can see what it means to so many people. It feels like there's thousands and thousands out on the field here," Carr told BBC Sport NI.

"Just to finally get over the line, it's more a sense of relief because I feel we've probably left a couple behind in the last few years. I mean, finals are just all about winning and thankfully we did that today.

"You know, it's ten years since we were in a final and I think there's seven people playing that are involved today that were involved then. So, caginess was probably to be expected.

"The first week back after the Carryduff game in the semi-final, training was cagey. So, maybe training translated right on to the field. But nerves are normal. No matter how cagey it was, I'm just glad we came out to the right side of it."

The season does not end here for Clonduff. They will now go to represent the county in the Ulster Club Championship, starting with a preliminary clash against the Tyrone winners on the weekend ending the 1 November.

Their opponents will be known after next Sunday's Red Hand decider, where Errigal Ciaran take on an Edendork side appearing in their first senior final.

"I was reminded there of an Ulster campaign that never came into anybody's head. So, it'll be back down there on Wednesday night. Get back to the tactics board and ready to go," said Carr.

"It's a massive honour. A massive honour for me and Stephen (McConville) to be up there on behalf of our players lifting the Cup.

"But to represent the county in Ulster is a massive honour for the whole group. Hopefully, we can give it a bit of a run, we'll take it one game at a time. The Tyrone Champions come out flying in Ulster, it's bonus territory for us."
